Orchot Tzadikim 25:9: The third: if he shames him before others for the deeds of his ancestors, of this our Sages of blessed memory said (Avot 3:11): whoever whitens the face of his fellow in public has no share in the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:10: The fourth: if he makes known the abominations of a person's ancestors before people, not in that person's presence, in order to shame him in people's eyes — of this they said: the group of slanderers does not receive the presence of the Divine Presence (Sotah 42a).
Orchot Tzadikim 25:11: The fifth: if the person is a repentant sinner, and one relates his former iniquities — for this there is a great punishment (Bava Metzia 58b), for one who repents of his iniquities has his iniquities turned into merits (Yerushalmi Peah 1:1), and this person shames him over transgressions that are actually merits. And further: he places a stumbling-block before him, for the repentant sinner will think in his heart: since he shames me, I too will shame him, and he will enter into strife with him, and through this he will be spoiled in his teshuvah and return to his former ways. And further: others who hear of this person's shame will be deterred and not do teshuvah, so it turns out that this one locks the gates of teshuvah. And know: if a man sees his fellow transgress a matter of Torah in private, and reveals it publicly, he has a sin in this, for perhaps the sinner has turned from his evil way. He should not reveal it except to a discreet sage, so as not to shame him, but merely distance himself from his company until it becomes known that he has turned from his evil way. And if the sinner is a Torah scholar, a man who fears sin, it is fitting to think clearly of him that he has done teshuvah, and if his inclination overpowered him once, he later regretted it.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:12: Whoever relates slander is punished for the harm he did his fellow, and there is a further punishment for rejoicing in his fellow's disgrace. And it is written (Leviticus 19:18), "and you shall love your fellow as yourself." And just as one loves his own honor, so should he love his fellow's honor. And it is written (Proverbs 17:5), "whoever rejoices at calamity shall not go unpunished."
Orchot Tzadikim 25:13: There is a side on which the iniquity of one who relates true slander is greater than one who relates falsehood: for when a person relates truthful things about his fellow, people will believe him, and it will remain a shame in their eyes even after he has repented and done teshuvah for his sin. But false slander — the whole world will understand it is false and not believe it. Yet in general, most matters of falsehood carry a greater punishment than truth.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:14: The sixth: one who relates slander about charity collectors who are honest, collecting faithfully and distributing to those who fear Heaven. Those who slander them, saying they steal the charity, or show favoritism and give to whomever they wish and to their relatives — this slander has a punishment beyond measure. For it causes those collectors to be removed, and other bad ones appointed in their place, so that good is withheld from those who give charity, and the good poor are robbed, for those other bad collectors will not have compassion on the good poor. It follows that this person has nullified the service of the Holy One, blessed be He, and shamed the servants of the Holy One, blessed be He, and their children and relatives, for instead of honoring them, it is not enough that he did not honor them, but he even did them harm. And he discourages other God-fearing people from becoming collectors, for they will think: why should we do something for which we will later be suspected, as so-and-so and so-and-so, God-fearing men, were suspected?
Orchot Tzadikim 25:15: And our Sages of blessed memory said (Arachin 15b): slander kills three people — the one who says it, the one who accepts it, and the one about whom it is said. And whoever accepts slander about his fellow is punished more than the one who says it. It is forbidden to dwell in the neighborhood of slanderers, how much more so to sit with them to hear their words.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:16: There is a further evil in slander: whoever relates slander about his fellow becomes proud, and regards himself as righteous in his own eyes, for he thinks: so-and-so did such-and-such, and I did not do it! It follows that he becomes proud and credits himself for good. And if he performed an actual commandment and credited himself for it, this would already be very bad — how much more so when he commits a great transgression through slander and credits himself for it. And if a person relates slander about orphans and widows, his punishment is even greater, for they are already grieving without this, and he grieves them still more.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:17: Whoever says to his fellow, "where is there fire? Only in the house of so-and-so, where meat and fish are usually found" — even this is slander (Arachin 15b). Come and see how careful a person must be about slander!
Orchot Tzadikim 25:18: There is also the dust of slander, such as saying, "be quiet about so-and-so, I do not wish to make known what I know about him." And the like of this. And our Sages of blessed memory further said (Arachin 16a): a person should not speak of his fellow's good qualities, for from his good qualities one may come to speak of his bad qualities. Its meaning: if you relate his good qualities before his enemy, the enemy will answer, "how can you praise him, when he does such-and-such?" And of this it is said, "he who blesses his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him" (Proverbs 27:14). But it is permitted before his own friends, as we learned (Avot 2:8): "Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai had five disciples, and he would enumerate their praises..." And likewise one who relates slander in a jesting and lighthearted manner, meaning that he does not speak out of hatred, is described by the verse (Proverbs 26:18-19), "as a madman who casts firebrands, arrows, and death, so is the man who deceives his neighbor, and says, am I not joking?"
Orchot Tzadikim 25:19: And likewise one who relates slander by way of hints, relating it innocently as though not knowing this is slander, but when rebuked says, "I did not know these were so-and-so's deeds, or that this is slander." One who relates things that cause harm to his fellow, whether to his body or his money, even merely to cause him grief or fear — this is slander. And whoever tells his fellow something is forbidden to reveal it without his permission (Yoma 4b). Anything said before three people is considered already known to all; and if one of the three relates it, there is no slander in it (Arachin 16a). But if he intends to spread it further, there is slander in it. And if the speaker warned the listeners not to reveal it, even if he said it before many people, there is slander in it. There is a story of a student who revealed something said in the study hall after twenty-two years, and they expelled him from the study hall, saying: this one reveals secrets (Sanhedrin 31a).
Orchot Tzadikim 25:20: There is further a transgression called talebearing. Who is a talebearer? One who goes from this person to that one and says, "I heard such-and-such about so-and-so!" — even if it is true, he thereby destroys the world. And we were warned of this, as it is written (Leviticus 19:16), "you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people." And what is talebearing? One who reveals to his fellow things said about him in private. And it is taught: from where do we learn that a judge should not say, "I would acquit, but my colleagues rule to convict — but what can I do, since my colleagues outnumber me?" Therefore it is said: "you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people." And it says (Proverbs 11:13), "a talebearer reveals secrets" (Sanhedrin 29a).
Orchot Tzadikim 25:21: Be very careful, my son, about slander, for by it you shame yourself. For whoever disqualifies others is himself disqualified. And he does not speak in praise of the world, for it is his way to find fault with people through his own flaw (Kiddushin 70a), for the flaw he himself has is placed in his heart all day, and since it is in his heart, he brings it out with his mouth. For every person is examined and recognized by his deeds. How so? If you see a person accustomed to praising women, and always speaking of them — know that he loves women. And if he praises fine foods and wine, and is accustomed to this — know that he is a glutton and a drunkard. And so with everything. And proof from the verse (Psalms 119:97), "how I love Your Torah! It is my meditation all the day" — because I love the Torah, I always speak of it. For whatever a person loves in his heart, he always speaks of it.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:22: The master of the [evil] tongue searches out people's flaws. And he is like flies, which always rest on a place of filth: if a person has a boil, flies will leave the rest of the body and settle on the boil. So it is with the master of slander: he leaves aside all the good in a person, and speaks of the bad. There is a story of a man who walked with a sage in a field and saw a carcass. That man said, "how putrid is this carcass!" The sage said, "how white are its teeth!" The sage rebuked that man and said: "why do you say its disgrace? Say its praise!" For a person should always speak in praise of the world.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:23: If you see a person say something or do something, and there is room to judge his words and deeds either toward guilt or toward merit: if he is a God-fearing man, you are obligated to judge him favorably in a truthful manner, even if the matter tends more toward guilt than merit. And if he is an average person, who is careful about sin but sometimes stumbles in it, you should incline the doubt and decide it in his favor, and the exalted Omnipresent will decide us favorably (Shabbat 127b). And this is a positive commandment from the Torah, as it is said (Leviticus 19:15), "in righteousness shall you judge your fellow." And if the matter tends toward guilt — if the man's deeds are mostly bad, and you know there is no fear of the exalted Lord in his heart — you should decide his words and deeds unfavorably.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:24: If a person reveals your sin, do not say, "just as he revealed my sin, I too will reveal his sin," for it is said (Leviticus 19:18), "you shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge." Nor should you boast, "even though he revealed [things] about me, I will not reveal [things] about him," for in this very statement you have already revealed half of it. And this matter is a great principle in the fear of Heaven. But if the sinner does not fear Heaven, such as one who has thrown off the yoke and is not careful about a certain transgression that all the people of his town know is a transgression — it is a commandment to relate his disgrace, to reveal his sins and to make the transgressors stink in people's eyes, so that the people hear and despise him, and keep themselves far from the transgressions, as it is said (Proverbs 29:27), "an unjust man is an abomination to the righteous." And it is said (ibid. 8:13), "the fear of the Lord is to hate evil." And they said (Sanhedrin 52a): a wicked man, son of a righteous man, may be called "wicked, son of a wicked man"; a righteous man, son of a wicked man, may be called "righteous, son of a righteous man." And it is specifically in this manner that one may shame him for the sake of Heaven. But whoever quarrels with him and intends to revile him solely for his own benefit, not for the sake of Heaven, should not reveal his sin. And likewise, if this revealer is himself a sinner, he should not reveal another sinner's transgression, for certainly he does not reveal secrets for a good purpose; "and a word of the lips leads only to want" (Proverbs 14:23).
Orchot Tzadikim 25:25: But there are a few occasions when slander is a commandment. For instance, two wicked men who plotted to do evil — it is permitted to reveal it as slander, and to cause them to hate one another and do evil to each other, so that they not do evil to the good. Likewise an adulterer pursuing an adulteress — it is a commandment to speak slander of it, so that they not commit the transgression. And sometimes, even when the sinner is completely wicked, one should not shame him publicly in a place where there is concern that he might turn to a fully wicked way of life. And it is permitted to relate slander about those who cause strife, as it is said (1 Kings 1:14), "and I will come in after you, and confirm your words" (Yerushalmi Peah 1:1).
Orchot Tzadikim 25:26: Because so many matters depend on the tongue, one must guard his tongue very carefully. Therefore David said (Psalms 34:14), "guard your tongue from evil." And our Sages of blessed memory said (Vayikra Rabbah 16:2): there is a story of a man who called out in the street, "who wishes to buy the elixir of life?" All the people came to buy, and he took out the Book of Psalms and showed them what is written in it: "who is the man who desires life, who loves days to see good? Guard your tongue from evil." And when Rabbi Yannai saw this, he brought him into his house, fed him and gave him drink, and gave him money. His students came and said to him: "until now did you not know this verse?" He said to them: "I knew it, but did not take it to heart to be careful of this matter. And when I would read this verse, I passed over it and did not concern myself, and this man came and fulfilled it for me — from now on I will be more careful with my tongue."
Orchot Tzadikim 25:27: Therefore, a person whose tongue is accustomed to flattery and mockery, and to relating slander, and to speaking falsehood and idle words, and who now wishes to submit and refrain from this, and to make a very great and strong fence — he should make a fence of distancing himself from his former companions, with whom he was accustomed to speak mockery, flattery, slander, and falsehood. For if he draws near them, he will not be able to refrain, for they will begin to speak with him as they are accustomed, and then he will not be able to restrain himself from speaking with them as he was accustomed. And he must accustom himself very, very much to silence, to accustom himself to open his mouth less; and he should sit alone in his room often and occupy himself with Torah, and associate with the pious who speak only of Torah and the fear of Heaven. And by accustoming himself to this for many days, he will find a remedy for his affliction.
Orchot Tzadikim 25:28: It is written (Proverbs 18:21), "death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who love it shall eat its fruit." There is a story of a king of Persia who fell ill. The physicians told him: "there is no remedy for you unless they bring you the milk of a lioness, and we will make a remedy for you from it." Then one man answered and said to him: "I will bring you the milk of a lioness if you wish, but give me ten goats." The king told his servant to give them to him, and they gave them to him. He went to the lions' den, where there was a lioness nursing her cubs. On the first day he stood far off and threw one goat, and she ate it. On the second day he came a little closer, and threw her another. And so he did every day until he was playing with her, and took some of her milk and left. When he was halfway home, he saw in a dream that all his limbs were quarreling with one another. The feet said: "none of the limbs compare to us, for had we not walked, he could not have brought milk from the lioness." And the hands said: "there is none like us, for had we not milked her, he could not have done anything." The eyes said: "we are above all, for had we not shown him the way, nothing would have been accomplished." The heart answered and said: "there is none like me — had I not given counsel, what would all of you have accomplished?" The tongue answered and said to them: "there is none like me, for had I not spoken the matter, who would have done it?" All the limbs answered it: "how are you not ashamed to compare yourself to us — are you not enclosed and placed in a place of darkness and gloom, and have no bone in you as the other limbs do?" The tongue said to them: "you shall see that I am king and rule over you."
Orchot Tzadikim 25:29: The man remembered these things. He went to the king and said to him: "my lord the king, here is dog's milk for you!" The king was furious and ordered him hanged. As he was being led to be hanged, the limbs began to weep. The tongue said to them: "did I not tell you that you have no substance in you?" And the tongue said: "if I save you, will you admit to me that I am king over you?" At once the tongue said: "take me back to the king, perhaps I will be saved." They brought him back to the king. He said to him: "why did you order me hanged? Is this the reward for such service?" He said to him: "because you brought me dog's milk." He said to him: "and what does it matter to you, if you have your remedy? And further: a lioness is also called a 'dog' [in a certain manner of speech]." They took it from him and tested it, and it was found to be lioness's milk. The limbs said to it: "now we acknowledge that you spoke the truth." And this is: "death and life are in the hand of the tongue" (Midrash Tehillim 32). Therefore David said (Psalms 39:2), "I will guard my ways, that I sin not with my tongue."
Orchot Tzadikim 25:30: See that the tongue is better than sacrifices, as it is said (Psalms 69:31-32), "I will praise the name of God with a song, and magnify Him with thanksgiving, and it shall please the Lord better than an ox or a bull with horns and hooves."
Orchot Tzadikim 25:31: You must reflect on and discern the matter of the tongue, for all of a person's affairs, for good and for bad, depend on it. A person can commit countless great and grave transgressions with the tongue, such as informing, talebearing, mockery, flattery, falsehood, and the like of these. And all these are great transgressions from which the master of the tongue gains nothing. And he can also perform countless commandments with his tongue. There are many people who say: what commandment can we perform? We have no money to give charity to the poor. And they do not know that the source of the commandments is very close to them — the source of life in this world and in the World to Come — and it is the tongue. And so David said: "who wishes to acquire this world and the World to Come?" They said to him: "no person can attain both." He said to them: "it is very cheap. And so it says: 'who is the man who desires life' (Psalms 34:13)." They said to him: "who can acquire life?" He said to them: "guard your tongue from evil" (ibid. verse 14).
Orchot Tzadikim 25:32: Let him accustom his tongue to speak words of Torah and fear of Heaven, and to rebuke people, and to command his children after him to keep and to do. And to comfort mourners, and comfort the poor, and speak good words of comfort to their hearts, and speak truth, and accustom himself to songs and praises. And then he will be beloved below and cherished above, and his reward will be in the great good hidden away for the righteous.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:2: Teshuvah. Rabbi Levi said: great is teshuvah, for it reaches the Throne of Glory, as it is said (Hosea 14:2), "Return, Israel, to the Lord your God" (Yoma 86a). And our Sages of blessed memory said: when Moses ascended to the first firmament, he found groups of angels. They opened before him a Torah scroll and read the account of the first day, then stopped and began to relate the praise of the Torah. He ascended to the second, and found companies of angels reading the account of the second day; they stopped and began to relate the praise of the Torah and of Israel. He ascended to the third, and found angels and troops reading the account of the third day; they stopped and began to relate the praise of Jerusalem. He ascended to the fourth, and found the Er'ellim reading the account of the fourth day; they stopped and began to relate the praise of the Messiah. He ascended to the fifth, and found camp upon camp reading the account of the fifth day; they stopped and began to relate the grief of Gehinnom. He ascended to the sixth, and found there angels reading the account of the sixth day; they stopped and began to relate the account of the Garden of Eden, requesting before the Holy One, blessed be He, to give Israel's portion in the Garden of Eden. He ascended to the seventh, and found ophanim and seraphim, celestial wheels and angels of mercy, angels of kindness and righteousness, and angels of trembling and shuddering. At once he took hold of the Throne of Glory. They began to read the account of the seventh day, "and they were finished," and stopped and began to relate the praise of teshuvah — to teach you that teshuvah reaches the Throne of Glory, as it is said, "Return, Israel, to the Lord your God" (Hosea 14:2).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:3: Rabbi Akiva said (Pesachim 54a): seven things preceded the world, and these are: Torah, teshuvah, the Garden of Eden and Gehinnom, the Throne of Glory, the Temple, and the name of the Messiah. And why these seven? Know that the essential purpose of the creation of the world was for man, for the lower world has need of nothing but man, and he rules over the entire lower world — over beasts, wild animals, birds, fish, and creeping things. And since the essential purpose of creation was for man, the Torah, which sustains the world, had to precede it, as it is written, "were it not for My covenant day and night, I would not have set the statutes of heaven and earth" (Jeremiah 33:25).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:4: And since the Torah preceded, teshuvah likewise had to precede, for since the Torah contains positive and negative commandments and punishments spelled out in the Torah, teshuvah had to precede in every case, so that if a person sinned he would have time to return; for otherwise the world would not have endured a single generation, for "there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin" (Ecclesiastes 7:20), and as soon as a generation sins it deserves to be destroyed and annihilated. And therefore the story of Sodom was written in the Torah, to make known to sinners that they deserve to be destroyed, they and all that is theirs, and that the earth too deserved to be overturned like Sodom, but the Holy One, blessed be He, made teshuvah precede, and waits generation after generation.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:5: And since Torah and teshuvah preceded, the Garden of Eden, Gehinnom, and the Throne of Glory likewise had to precede, for these are places to repay a man according to his deeds.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:6: And since all these preceded, the Temple and the name of the Messiah had to precede likewise, for in those days the earth will be filled with knowledge, and there will be no evil inclination among people, and all will know that the essential purpose of the creation of the world was for the service of the exalted Creator. Therefore these seven preceded the world. "And saviors shall come up on Mount Zion" (Obadiah 1:21), "and a redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those who turn from transgression in Jacob" (Isaiah 59:20). Amen, and may it be His will.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:7: Because of seven things, a person should hasten to return in his youth, while he is in the fullness of his strength. The first: because the service of Torah and fear, and all the virtues a person is obligated in, are very, very many. Of this it is said, "its measure is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea" (Job 11:9). "And the day is short" (Mishnah Avot 2:15), for this world is a very short day, "our days on earth are as a shadow" (1 Chronicles 29:15). And our Sages of blessed memory said (Bereishit Rabbah 96:2): not like the shadow of a wall, nor the shadow of a tree, but like the shadow of a bird flying in the air. "And the workers are lazy" — this is the person who has the trait of laziness.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:8: And now consider: a person obligated to walk a day's journey of ten parasangs or more, and the road is full of obstacles of mud and stones, and there are bandits and murderers on that road, and he must go regardless, because the king has so commanded him and he cannot refuse — how much must such a person hasten in the morning and gird his loins with diligence and walk swiftly. Therefore one should rise early and hasten to the service of the exalted Creator. And even when he does all he is capable of, he attains only a little of the virtues. As our Sages said (Avot d'Rabbi Natan 16:4) on what is written, "for He knows our inclination" (Psalms 103:14): a parable of a king who gave a field to his servants, and told them to work it and guard it, and bring from it thirty kor each year. And they toiled over it and worked it well, and brought before the king five kor. He said to them: what is this you have done? They said to him: our lord the king, the field you gave us is poor soil, and we worked it with all our strength, and it produced no more than this amount. So it is with a person: even when he serves with all his strength, his service is small. And if he says, I will wait until I am free and until I earn enough for my needs — behold, the world's preoccupations never cease, and as our Sages of blessed memory said: "do not say, when I am free I will study, lest you never become free" (Mishnah Avot 2:4).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:9: The second: if he delays his teshuvah until he brings in and gathers wealth, he will then covet and yearn for still more, as our Sages of blessed memory said (Kohelet Rabbah 1:13): no person leaves this world with even half his desire fulfilled; if he has a hundred, he desires to make two hundred; if he attains two hundred, he desires to make four hundred. And so the verse says: "he who loves money shall not be satisfied with money" (Ecclesiastes 5:9).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:10: The third: time is diminishing while the work is abundant — the work of Torah, the improvement of the soul, and the attainment of virtues such as the fear [of Heaven].
Orchot Tzadikim 26:11: The fourth: when he delays improving his soul, the evil inclination continues to grow powerful, and his heart hardens, and he becomes accustomed to transgressions, and all transgressions become in his eyes as though permitted, and he will be unable to purify himself.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:12: The fifth: whoever does not wish to hasten to return, perhaps he will not live long and will die before he returns; therefore it was warned, "let your garments always be white" (Ecclesiastes 9:8).
Orchot Tzadikim 26:13: The sixth: when he delays returning, his iniquities become old, and he will forget them and not worry over them as he did at first.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:14: The seventh: when he comes into old age and the strength of his inclination weakens, he will not receive reward for his teshuvah as though he had done teshuvah in his youth, when he was in the fullness of his strength. And because of these seven things, a person should hasten to improve his soul before the exalted King.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:15: And after it arises in a person's heart to do teshuvah, he cannot do complete teshuvah unless he takes seven things to heart. The first: that he know his deeds and recall them all. For a person who was not accustomed to fulfilling the commandments from his youth will commit transgressions all his days. And many people suppose that a person is not called a "repentant sinner" unless he has had relations with a married woman or a gentile woman, or has taken up a wicked way of life, and the like of these great transgressions; but regarding other transgressions they do not know that one must repent of them. But this is not so, for regarding everything our Sages warned about, it is more severe than the words of the Torah, for whoever transgresses the words of the Sages is liable for death (Berachot 4b). And whoever transgresses the words of the Torah or the words of the Sages must repent.
Orchot Tzadikim 26:16: And now hear, my son, that most of the world is not careful about idle talk, and about gazing at women, and speaking with them without need. Also they are not careful to pray with intent, and about talking in the synagogue, and about laughter and levity. Also they are not careful about giving charity to whoever deserves it, and about hardening their heart and closing their hand, and speaking harsh words to the poor. Also they are not careful about vain oaths, and cursing their fellow or themselves by the Name; and mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain, or in an unclean place, or with unclean hands; and idleness from Torah study is worse than all of these.
